column2: Having taken the form of Narasimha, with the gods he slew him, who had won the gods' share of sacrifice and made himself master over all the gods.
Praised by the gods, Narasimha restored the gods to their own stations. In the ancient war of gods and demons, led by Bali and others,
the gods, defeated and fallen from heaven, took refuge in Hari. Having given the gods fearlessness, with Aditi and Kashyapa,
praised by them, he became Vamana, born of Aditi, and went to the sacrifice of Bali, the glorious sacrificer; at the king's door he recited the Veda.
Hearing him recite the gods' hymns, the boon-giving Bali said to Vamana, though forbidden by Shukra, "Say what you desire.
I shall give you that," Vamana said to Bali: "Give me three steps for my teacher's sake," and he replied, "I shall give."
When water fell on his hand, Vamana became no longer small; he made the three steps — the earth, the middle world and heaven.
Hari made Bali king of Sutala and gave the three worlds to Indra. Indra, praising Hari with the gods, became happy as lord of the world.
I shall tell the descent of Parashurama; listen, O twice-born. Considering the Kshatriyas arrogant, for removing the earth's burden,
Hari descended for peace as protector of gods and Brahmins: Bhargava, born of Jamadagni and Renuka, master of weapons.
By Dattatreya's grace there was a king Kartavirya, thousand-armed, lord of all the earth; he went hunting.
Wearied, he was invited in the forest by the sage Jamadagni; by the power of the wish-fulfilling cow, the king with his army was fed.
When he asked for the wish-fulfilling cow and the sage did not give it, he took it away; then Rama cut off his head and felled him.
In battle the king was killed with the axe; the cow returned to her own hermitage. But by Kartavirya's sons Jamadagni was slain.
When Rama had gone to the forest, out of enmity... then Rama came back; seeing his father slain, enraged at his father's killing,
the mighty one made the earth free of Kshatriyas three times seven times. At Kurukshetra, having made five pools and satisfied the ancestors,
having given the earth to Kashyapa, he stayed on Mount Mahendra. Hearing of the avatars of Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana and Rama, a man goes to heaven.
Rama and the others were equal to their father, nourished by the sacrifice; for the destruction of the obstacles to the sacrifice, the king, requested by Vishvamitra,
sent Rama with Lakshmana along with the sage. Rama went, was taught weapons and missiles, and killed Tataka.
With the human missile he sent Maricha, bewildered, far away; the mighty one slew Subahu, destroyer of the sacrifice, with his army.
Dwelling at Siddhashrama with Vishvamitra and others, he went with his younger brother to see the sacrifice of the king of Mithila and the bow.
Through Shatananda, glorified by Vishvamitra, he was described to Rama by the king, and the sage was honored at the sacrifice.
He strung the bow in play and broke it. Janaka, whose daughter Sita, born of no womb, was to be won by valor,
gave her to Rama; and when the father and others arrived, Rama wed Janaki, and Lakshmana wed Urmila.
Shrutakirti and Mandavi, the daughters of Kushadhvaja, the younger brother of Janaka — Shatrughna and Bharata, both,
wed the two maidens, well honored by Janaka. Rama went with Vasishtha and others after conquering Jamadagni's son; Bharata came to Ayodhya with Shatrughna and Yudhajit.
He saw Kaikeyi angry and said, "Why are you thus? Are you sick, afraid or troubled? What do you wish? I shall do it."
Without Rama I cannot live even a moment; I swear by him, I shall do what you desire, fair one.
Speak the truth, she said: "If you give me, O king, the two boons given before, give them to me, O king, by your truth.
Let Rama live in the forest, restrained, for fourteen years; with these preparations let Bharata be anointed here today.
If you do not, O king, I shall drink poison and die." Hearing that, he fell fainting to the ground as if struck by a thunderbolt.
After a moment regaining consciousness, he said to Kaikeyi: "What has Rama done to you, or I, O sinful one,
that you speak to me thus, disliked by the whole world? Only by doing what pleases you shall I be greatly blamed.
You, wife, a night of death — Bharata is not such a son. Rule as a widow when I am dead and my son gone."
Bound by the noose of truth, he called Rama and said: "Rama, cheated by Kaikeyi, restrain me and rule the kingdom.
You must live in the forest; let Bharata and Kaikeyi be king." Having saluted his father and Kaikeyi, with circumambulation,
having bowed to Kaushalya and comforted her, with Lakshmana, together with his wife Sita, with chariot and Sumantra,
having given gifts to Brahmins, the poor and the helpless, he left the city, with mothers and Brahmins and others sorrowing.
Having spent the night on the bank of the Tamasa and leaving the citizens, at dawn those who did not see him returned to Ayodhya.
The king too, weeping, deeply sorrowful, went to Kaushalya's house; the citizens, women and all the king's wives wept.
Rama, riding in his chariot, clad in bark, went to Shringaverapura; honored by Guha there, he rested under an ingudi tree.
Lakshmana and Guha kept vigil in the night; leaving Sumantra with the chariot, in the morning they crossed the Ganga by boat.
Rama, Lakshmana and Sita crossed and reached Prayaga; saluting Bharadvaja, they went to Mount Chitrakuta.
Having then performed the house-site worship, they stayed on the bank of the Mandakini; Rama showed Chitrakuta to Sita.
The crow, tearing her with its claws, struck at her eye; by a blade-of-grass missile it sought refuge and went through the sky, abandoning the gods.
When Rama had gone to the forest, on the sixth day at night the king told Kaushalya the earlier story of what he had once done through ignorance.
In youth, on the bank of the Sarayu, the boy Yajnadatta, by confusion of the sound, making the sound with a pitcher, his father
lamented and cursed him with his mother, weeping again and again in grief: "You too will die of sorrow, without your son, as we shall die."
Remembering that, Kaushalya, my death will be from grief without my son. Having told the tale and cried "Ah Rama," the king went to heaven.
Thinking him asleep, Kaushalya slept, herself sorrow-stricken; in the early morning the singers, bards, heralds and praise-singers
awakened him, but he did not wake, being dead. Knowing him dead, Kaushalya cried "Alas, I am slain!"
Men and women wept; Bharata was then brought quickly from Rajagriha to the city with Shatrughna by Vasishtha and others.
Seeing Kaikeyi grieved, he censured her in sorrow; dishonor was placed on her head, and he praised Kaushalya.
Having performed the rites for his father, placed in an oil vessel, on the bank of the Sarayu, told by Vasishtha and others to rule, he said:
I shall go to bring Rama; Rama is the strong king acknowledged. At Shringavera and Prayaga he was fed by Bharadvaja.
Saluting Bharadvaja, he came to Rama and Lakshmana: "Father has gone to heaven, Rama; be king in Ayodhya.
I shall go to the forest awaiting your command." Hearing it, Rama gave water offerings and said, "Take my sandals and go.

I shall not come back for the kingdom, bound by truth, wearing bark and matted hair." Told by Rama, Bharata came and, the strong one, stayed at Nandigrama; leaving Ayodhya, he honored the sandals and guarded the kingdom.
Khara said "So be it" to her, and with fourteen thousand Rakshasas, with Dushana, he came to fight with Trishiras.
Rama also fought, piercing the Rakshasas with arrows; he sent their army of elephants, horses, chariots and infantry to Yama's abode.
Trishiras, terrible Khara and Dushana, fighting — Shurpanakha went to Lanka and fell on the ground before Ravana.
Angry, she said to Ravana: "You are not a king nor a protector. Take Sita, the wife of Rama, the slayer of Khara and others.
I live by drinking the blood of Rama and Lakshmana, not otherwise." He said "So be it," and heard it, then said to Maricha, "Go,
become a golden spotted deer, luring Rama and Lakshmana; I shall carry off Sita in front of them, otherwise you will die."
Maricha said to Ravana: "Rama, the archer, is death; I must die by Ravana too, I must die by Rama too.
If I must die in any case, better Rama than Ravana." Thinking so, as a deer he wandered repeatedly before Sita.
Urged by Sita, Rama then slew him with an arrow. Dying, the deer cried "Ah Sita, ah Lakshmana!"
Told by Sita, Lakshmana went to Rama, who was upset; Ravana too abducted Sita, killing the vulture Jatayu.
With his body torn by Jatayu, he took Janaki on his lap, went to Lanka, and held her in the Ashoka grove, saying:
Be my chief wife; let the Rakshasis guard her. Rama, having slain Maricha, saw Lakshmana and said:
That was a magic deer, Lakshmana; as you have come here, so surely Sita has been taken. He went and did not see her.
He grieved and lamented in pain: "Leaving me, where have you gone?" Comforted by Lakshmana, Rama searched for Janaki.
Seeing Jatayu, who told him that Ravana had taken her, and when he died he was cremated by him; then he killed Kabandha, who, freed from a curse, said to Rama: "Go to Sugriva."
At Rishyamuka the lord of Kishkindha said to the lord of monkeys: "As you shall obtain Sita, so I shall do for you, Rama."
Hearing that, he kept the Chaturmasya on the ridge of Malyavan. When Sugriva did not come to be seen at Kishkindha,
Lakshmana said to him, told by Rama: "Go to Rama. The way by which Bali went when slain is not narrowed.
Keep to the agreement, Sugriva; do not follow Bali's path." Sugriva said, attached to pleasure, "I did not realize time had passed."
So saying, the lord of monkeys went and bowed to Rama and said: "All the monkeys have been brought for the search for Sita.
By your leave I shall send them to search for Janaki; let them come in a month from the east and other quarters; after a month I shall kill them."
So told, the monkeys went on the eastern, western and northern roads and returned to Rama with Sugriva, not having seen Janaki.
Taking Rama's ring, Hanuman with the monkeys searched in the south near Suprabha's cave.
Placed beyond the month, not seeing Janaki, they said: "We shall die in vain; Jatayu is blessed,
who gave up his life for Sita, slain by Ravana in battle." Hearing that, Sampati said, leaving off eating the monkeys:

That Jatayu is my brother; I flew to the orb of the sun; he was protected from the sun's heat and went; I, my wings burnt, fell from the sky.
agnipuran:8:15	By hearing the news of Rama my wings grew again. Now I see Janaki, who is in the Ashoka grove, in Lanka,
agnipuran:8:16	in the salt sea a hundred yojanas wide, on Trikuta. Having known this, let the monkeys tell Rama with Sugriva.
He did not see Sita in the drinking-halls and other places, absorbed in anxiety. Going to the Ashoka grove, he saw her under a shimshapa tree.
Sita, guarded by Rakshasis, and Ravana saying "Be my wife"; the monkey on the shimshapa tree saw her answer "No."
The Rakshasis said "Be Ravana's wife"; the monkey, when Ravana had gone, said: "There was a king Dasharatha;
Rama and Lakshmana are his two excellent sons gone to forest-dwelling; you, wife of Rama, Janaki, were taken by force by Ravana.
Rama, the friend of Sugriva, searching for you, sent me. Take this ring given by Rama as a token."
She took Sita's ring... she saw Hanuman, and when he sat again before her she said, "Is he alive?"
Why does Rama not take me away? she asked, doubting. The monkey said: "Rama does not know, Sita; knowing you are here he will take you.
Having slain Ravana the Rakshasa with his army, do not grieve, goddess. Give me a token." Sita gave the monkey a jewel.
She said: "Act so that Rama takes me quickly. Tell the tale of the crow striking my eye; go back, remover of grief."
Taking the jewel and the tale, Hanuman said, "Your husband will take you. Or if you are in haste, climb on my back, auspicious one.
Today I shall show you Rama with Sugriva." Sita said to Hanuman, "Let Rama take me."
Hanuman made a plan to see Ravana: he broke the grove and slew its guards with teeth and nails.
Having slain all the servants, seven sons of ministers, and the son Aksha, Kumara and Indrajit bound him.
With the serpent noose he showed the tawny-eyed one to Ravana. Ravana said, "Who are you?" Maruti replied to Ravana.
